title: Library
intro: Texts for wider reading on Billy Budd: the editions, its sources and naval history, the Somers affair, Melville’s reading, the criticism and the adaptations. Open texts are held here; the rest link to where they are published, and the group keeps copies of some. Each entry gives its licence.

items.title: On Revolution
items.author: Arendt, Hannah
items.note: Arendt's comparative study of the American and French revolutions (first published by Viking, New York, 1963; Faber and Faber, London, 1964). Where it treats Billy Budd, in chapter 2, 'The Social Question' (pages of the Penguin reprint, 1990; the index gives pp. 80-88 and 101). p. 82: Melville and Dostoevsky return Jesus to the world of men, the one in Billy Budd, the other in 'The Grand Inquisitor'; absolute goodness is as dangerous as absolute evil, and lies beyond even Vere's virtue. p. 83: Melville answers the French Revolution's claim that man is good by nature; the story's topic is goodness beyond virtue and evil beyond vice; Billy and Claggart both come from outside society; Billy's blow is adequate to Claggart's depravity. p. 84: Vere brings in virtue, and the tragedy begins; the law, made for men, must punish elemental goodness; an absolute, for Melville embodied in the Rights of Man, spells doom in politics. pp. 84-85: envy here is Claggart's of Billy, not the poor's of the rich; the victim Billy feels compassion for Vere. p. 86: Billy's blessing of Vere ends the story on compassion and is nearer a gesture than speech; his stammer and Jesus's silence show compassion's incapacity for argument, so it cannot found lasting institutions. pp. 87-88: Billy can only strike; Melville reverses Cain and Abel, as the Revolution reversed original sin; the question comes from Melville's preface, on how the Revolution itself became a wrong-doer. p. 101: Melville's question on envy, echoed in a discussion of hypocrisy.

items.title: Justice Accused: Antislavery and the Judicial Process
items.author: Cover, Robert M.
items.note: Cover's study of antislavery judges who enforced the fugitive slave laws, first published by Yale University Press in 1975. Its opening, 'Prelude: Of Creon and Captain Vere' (pp. 1-7), uses Captain Vere as the type of the judge bound by positive law against conscience, and sets him beside Melville's father-in-law, Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw. Linked here at the publisher's digital edition (De Gruyter).

items.title: Melville's Fist: The Execution of "Billy Budd"
items.author: Johnson, Barbara
items.note: Deconstructive reading in Studies in Romanticism, vol. 18, no. 4, 'The Rhetoric of Romanticism' (Winter 1979), pp. 567-599, treating Billy and Claggart as figures of reading and Vere's verdict as an act of interpretation. items.title: Billy Budd and Other Prose Pieces (The Works of Herman Melville, vol. 13)
items.author: Melville, Herman; Weaver, Raymond M.
items.note: First printing of Billy Budd, as "Billy Budd, Foretopman", edited by Raymond M. Weaver as volume XIII of the Constable Standard Edition of Melville's works (London, Bombay, Sydney: Constable, 1924; limited to 750 copies; viii, 399 pages). Weaver's introductory note calls Billy Budd "a novel finished by Melville five months before his death" and describes "Daniel Orme" as a sketch "omitted from Billy Budd"; the volume also prints the Burgundy Club sketches and other late prose from the manuscripts. The Internet Archive copy is from the library of King Alfred's College, Winchester.

items.title: Billy Budd, Sailor (An Inside Narrative): Reading Text and Genetic Text
items.author: Melville, Herman; Hayford, Harrison; Sealts, Merton M., Jr.
items.note: Harrison Hayford and Merton M. Sealts Jr.'s edition "edited from the manuscript with introduction and notes" (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1962; ix, 431 pages, facsimiles, tables), giving a reading text and a genetic text of the manuscript. MEL notes that its foliation of the leaves was applied by Houghton in pencil to each recto and that it distinguished stages of composition. The reading text was also issued in 1962 as a Phoenix paperback without the genetic text.

items.title: Reading Billy Budd
items.author: Parker, Hershel
items.note: Book-length reading of the novella (Northwestern University Press, 1990; vi, 190 p.) built on the Hayford-Sealts Genetic Text, following the work's growth from the ballad 'Billy in the Darbies' through the later expansions and placing it in Melville's last years. HathiTrust holds a search-only copy (mdp.39015019420192).

items.title: Epistemology of the Closet
items.author: Sedgwick, Eve Kosofsky
items.note: Sedgwick's study of the modern homo/heterosexual definition, published by the University of California Press, Berkeley, in 1990. Chapter 2, 'Some Binarisms (I). Billy Budd: After the Homosexual', reads Claggart's 'depravity' and the novella's narrative reticence through the epistemology of the closet. An updated edition with a new preface appeared in 2008 (ISBN 9780520254060).

items.title: Proceedings of the court of inquiry appointed to inquire into the intended mutiny on board the United States brig of war Somers, on the high seas: held on board the United States ship North Carolina lying at the Navy Yard, New-York: with a full account of the execution of Spencer, Cromwell and Small, on board said vessel
items.author: United States. Navy. Court of Inquiry (Mackenzie : 1842); Mackenzie, Alexander Slidell
items.note: Report of the naval court of inquiry held aboard the USS North Carolina at the New York Navy Yard, "reported for The New-York Tribune" and printed by its publishers. It gives Mackenzie's narrative of the Somers affair as read to the court, in which Lieutenant Guert Gansevoort carries out Spencer's arrest and guards the prisoners, with testimony from members of the crew and an account of the three executions. Harvard University copy digitised by Google, 61 page images. Billy Budd's narrator, comparing Vere's court with the Somers case, calls Mackenzie's act one "vindicated by a naval court of inquiry subsequently convened ashore."
